CHAPTER 4.2 · LEARNING AREA 4 · APRIL · MAY

Prisms

Chocolate box, tent, pencil, honeycomb: many solids have two identical, parallel bases with rectangles in between – they are prisms. In this chapter you draw prisms as an oblique drawing and as a net, calculate surface area and volume, find their mass with the density and compare packaging.

16 LESSONS4 UNITS2 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • recognise prisms and represent them as an oblique drawing, in a two-view drawing and as a net
  • calculate the surface area and volume of right prisms and investigate how they change
  • use the density to get from volume to mass and back
  • calculate composite solids and compare packaging by the material it uses

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Representing prisms

A right prism has two identical, parallel polygons as its base and top face. The side faces are rectangles; together they are called the lateral surface. According to the base, we speak of triangular, quadrilateral, pentagonal or hexagonal prisms.

In an oblique drawing you draw the front face in its true size and the edges going back at 45° and half as long. In a two-view drawing the plan view (from above) and the front view (from the front) are one above the other, connected by construction lines.

A net consists of the two bases and the lateral surface. Unrolled, the lateral surface is a rectangle: as long as the perimeter of the base and as high as the prism.

KEY POINT · PRISM WITH AN n-GON AS ITS BASE

Vertices: $2n$ · edges: $3n$ · faces: $n + 2$

Oblique drawing: front in true size, going back at 45° and half the length, hidden edges dashed

Net: 2 bases and a lateral surface of $n$ rectangles

Lying down: a tent is a triangular prism lying down. The “height” of the prism is then its length.

Glue flaps are not part of the net, but every real piece of packaging has them.

INTERACTIVE · OBLIQUE DRAWING AND TWO-VIEW DRAWING

Choose a prism. Switch between the oblique drawing and the two-view drawing. Which edges are hidden?

INTERACTIVE · THE NET FOLDS UP

Drag the slider: the net folds up into the solid. Count the vertices, edges and faces.

EXAMPLE 1 · COUNTING

How many vertices, edges and faces does a hexagonal prism have?

$n = 6$: vertices $2 \cdot 6$, edges $3 \cdot 6$, faces $6 + 2$.

12 vertices, 18 edges, 8 faces

EXAMPLE 2 · THE LATERAL SURFACE AS A RECTANGLE

A triangular prism has a triangle with the sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm as its base and is 10 cm high. How big is the rectangle of the lateral surface?

Length = perimeter $3 + 4 + 5 = 12$ cm, height 10 cm.

12 cm × 10 cm

EXERCISES

Give the vertices, edges and faces: a) triangular prism   b) pentagonal prism   c) octagonal prism

a) 6, 9, 5   b) 10, 15, 7   c) 16, 24, 10

Draw the oblique drawing of a cuboid 4 cm wide, 3 cm deep and 2 cm high. How long do you draw the depth?

The depth is halved: 1.5 cm at 45°.

Draw the net of a triangular prism whose base is an equilateral triangle with a 3 cm side and which is 5 cm high. How big is the lateral surface?

Lateral surface 9 cm × 5 cm, so 45 cm². The two triangles sit on two sides of the rectangle.

In a two-view drawing, a solid looks like a hexagon from above and like a rectangle from the front. Which solid could it be?

A standing hexagonal prism, for example a pencil without a point.

A prism has 30 edges. How many vertices and faces does it have? What kind of polygon is the base?

$3n = 30$, so $n = 10$: a decagon. 20 vertices, 12 faces.

TEST YOURSELF!

Vertices of a pentagonal prism?

$2 \cdot 5 = 10$

Edges of a hexagonal prism?

$3 \cdot 6 = 18$

Oblique drawing: a depth of 4 cm is drawn as … cm?

$4 : 2 = 2$

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Surface area and volume of prisms

If you stack identical plates on top of each other, you get a prism. Each layer has the area of the base $G$, and there are as many layers as the prism is high. That is why: volume = base times height.

The surface area is the area of the net: twice the base plus the lateral surface. The lateral surface is a rectangle made of the perimeter of the base and the height.

With the formulas you can investigate how the volume and the surface area change: if you double the height, the volume doubles. If you double all the edges of the base, $G$ becomes four times as big – and so does $V$.

KEY POINT · PRISM

Volume: $V = G \cdot h$

Lateral surface: $M = u \cdot h$ · surface area: $O = 2 \cdot G + M$

Dependencies: $V$ is proportional to $h$ · double the base edges → four times the base

Units: 1 m³ = 1000 dm³ = 1,000,000 cm³ · 1 dm³ = 1 litre.

On the computer: in a spreadsheet you can change $h$ in steps and calculate $V$ – the graph is a straight line through the origin.

INTERACTIVE · CALCULATING PRISMS

Choose a base and change the edge and the height. Watch how $G$, $M$, $O$ and $V$ change.

EXAMPLE 3 · CALCULATING

A prism has a right-angled triangle with the sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm as its base and is 5 cm high. Calculate $V$ and $O$.

$G = 6 \cdot 8 : 2 = 24$ cm², $V = 24 \cdot 5 = 120$ cm³. $u = 24$ cm, $M = 24 \cdot 5 = 120$ cm², $O = 48 + 120 = 168$ cm².

V = 120 cm³, O = 168 cm²

EXAMPLE 4 · TENT

A tent (without a groundsheet) is 2 m wide and 1.5 m high at the front, the sloping sides are 1.8 m long each, and the length is 3 m. How much tent fabric do you need?

Two triangles: $2 \cdot (2 \cdot 1.5 : 2) = 3$ m². Two roof surfaces: $2 \cdot 1.8 \cdot 3 = 10.8$ m².

13.8 m²

EXERCISES

Calculate the volume: a) $G = 26$ cm², $h = 10$ cm   b) trapezium prism with $a = 8$ cm, $c = 4$ cm, height of the trapezium 3 cm, length 12 cm   c) triangular prism $g = 5$ cm, $h_\Delta = 4$ cm, height 9 cm

a) 260 cm³   b) $18 \cdot 12 = 216$ cm³   c) $10 \cdot 9 = 90$ cm³

A chocolate box is a triangular prism: an equilateral triangle with a 4 cm side (area about 7 cm²), length 20 cm. Calculate the volume and the surface area.

$V \approx 7 \cdot 20 = 140$ cm³. $O \approx 2 \cdot 7 + 12 \cdot 20 = 254$ cm².

A prism has $G = 6$ cm². Make a table for $h = 1,\, 2,\, 3,\, 4$ cm. How does $V$ depend on $h$?

6; 12; 18; 24 cm³. $V$ is proportional to $h$ with the factor 6.

A swimming pool is a trapezium prism lying down: 10 m long, 4 m wide, 1 m deep at one end and 2 m at the other. How much water fits in?

Cross-section (side wall) as a trapezium: $\tfrac{1 + 2}{2} \cdot 10 = 15$ m², width 4 m: $V = 60$ m³ = 60,000 litres.

All the edges of a hexagonal prism are doubled. How do the base, the volume and the surface area change?

The base and the rectangles of the lateral surface become four times as big, and so does $O$. The volume becomes $4 \cdot 2 = 8$ times as big.

TEST YOURSELF!

$G = 24$ cm², $h = 5$ cm: $V$ in cm³?

$24 \cdot 5 = 120$

$G = 24$ cm², $u = 24$ cm, $h = 5$ cm: $O$ in cm²?

$48 + 120 = 168$

All edges doubled: how many times as big does the volume become?

$2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 8$

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Mass and density

A wooden cube and an iron cube of the same size have the same volume, but the iron cube is much heavier. How heavy 1 cm³ of a material is, is given by its density $\varrho$ (pronounced “rho”).

Water has the density $1\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$: 1 cm³ weighs 1 g, 1 litre weighs 1 kg. Iron has about $7.9\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$, wood only about $0.5\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$. A solid floats in water if its density is less than that of water.

Mass, volume and density are connected by a formula. You can rearrange it for each quantity – as in chapter 3.3.

KEY POINT · DENSITY

$\varrho = \dfrac{m}{V}$   ·   $m = \varrho \cdot V$   ·   $V = \dfrac{m}{\varrho}$

Units: $1\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3} = 1\,\tfrac{\text{kg}}{\text{dm}^3} = 1\,\tfrac{\text{t}}{\text{m}^3}$

Values: water 1 · ice 0.92 · wood ≈ 0.5 · concrete ≈ 2.4 · aluminium 2.7 · iron 7.9 · gold 19.3 (in $\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$)

Measuring the volume of irregular solids: dip them into a measuring jug of water; the rise is the volume.

Physics in Year 6: there you already measured density. Here you calculate with prisms.

INTERACTIVE · HOW HEAVY IS THE CUBOID?

Choose a material and change the edges. Volume and mass are calculated straight away.

EXAMPLE 5 · MASS

An aluminium cuboid measures 10 cm × 5 cm × 4 cm. How heavy is it?

$V = 200$ cm³, $m = 2.7 \cdot 200 = 540$ g.

540 g

EXAMPLE 6 · DENSITY

A stone weighs 600 g. In the measuring jug the water rises by 240 cm³. What is its density?

$\varrho = \dfrac{600}{240} = 2.5$

$2.5\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$

EXERCISES

An iron bar is a prism with $G = 4$ cm² and a length of 50 cm. How heavy is it?

$V = 200$ cm³, $m = 7.9 \cdot 200 = 1580$ g ≈ 1.6 kg.

Does it float or sink? a) ice   b) aluminium   c) wood   d) concrete

a) floats   b) sinks   c) floats   d) sinks

A concrete slab is 2 m long, 1 m wide and 10 cm thick. How heavy is it?

$V = 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 0.1 = 0.2$ m³, $m = 2.4 \cdot 0.2 = 0.48$ t = 480 kg.

A gold bar weighs 1 kg. How big is its volume? Compare it with a matchbox (about 5 cm × 3.5 cm × 1.5 cm).

$V = 1000 : 19.3 \approx 51.8$ cm³. The box has about 26 cm³ – the bar is only about twice as big.

An aquarium (60 cm × 30 cm × 40 cm) weighs 15 kg empty. May it go on a shelf that holds 80 kg if it is three quarters full?

Volume 72 litres, three quarters of it 54 litres of water = 54 kg. Together 69 kg – that works (without stones and sand).

TEST YOURSELF!

200 cm³ of aluminium: mass in g?

$2.7 \cdot 200 = 540$

600 g and 240 cm³: density in g/cm³?

$600 : 240 = 2.5$

0.2 m³ of concrete (2.4 t/m³): mass in kg?

$0.48$ t

UNIT 44 LESSONS

4Composite solids and packaging

A house with a gable roof consists of a cuboid and a triangular prism lying down. A concrete step is a prism with a base shaped like an “L”. You calculate solids like these by splitting them into known parts.

Sometimes it is easier to see a solid as a prism with a composite base: first split the base, then multiply by the height. For hollow solids you calculate outside minus inside.

Packaging should hold a lot and use little material. For the same volume a cube needs less material than a long, flat cuboid – and small single portions need much more altogether than one big pack.

KEY POINT · COMPOSITE SOLIDS

Splitting: $V = V_1 + V_2$ · completing: $V = V_\text{large} - V_\text{missing}$ · hollow solids: outside minus inside

Prism with a composite base: $V = (G_1 + G_2) \cdot h$

Surface area: only the faces on the outside count

Sustainable: less packaging material means less waste. A returnable jar needs material once and is filled many times.

Project: compare packaging from the supermarket: content, surface area, material per 100 g of content.

EXAMPLE 7 · HOUSE

The bottom of a house is a cuboid (10 m long, 8 m wide, 6 m high). The roof is a triangular prism with the gable triangle $g = 8$ m, $h = 3$ m and a length of 10 m. How big is the enclosed volume?

Cuboid $10 \cdot 8 \cdot 6 = 480$ m³, roof $12 \cdot 10 = 120$ m³.

600 m³

EXAMPLE 8 · CONCRETE STEPS

Two steps: the lower one is 40 cm deep and 20 cm high, the upper one 20 cm deep and 20 cm high. The steps are 1 m wide. How much concrete do you need, and how heavy is it?

Base $40 \cdot 20 + 20 \cdot 20 = 1200$ cm², $V = 1200 \cdot 100 = 120{,}000$ cm³ = 0.12 m³. Mass $2.4 \cdot 0.12 = 0.288$ t.

0.12 m³, about 288 kg

EXERCISES

A solid consists of a cube with a 4 cm edge with a cuboid of 4 cm × 2 cm × 3 cm standing on it. Calculate the volume.

$64 + 24 = 88$ cm³

One litre of juice: compare the surface area of a cube (10 cm × 10 cm × 10 cm) with that of a cuboid (20 cm × 10 cm × 5 cm). Which needs less material?

Cube 600 cm², cuboid $2 \cdot (200 + 100 + 50) = 700$ cm². The cube saves material.

A window box measures 80 cm × 20 cm × 20 cm on the outside and 76 cm × 16 cm × 18 cm on the inside. How much material is in the walls? How much soil fits in?

Outside 32,000 cm³, inside 21,888 cm³. Material: 10,112 cm³ ≈ 10.1 dm³. Soil: about 21.9 litres.

One litre of juice is filled into 8 cubes with a 5 cm edge instead of one cube with a 10 cm edge. How much more material do you need?

One large cube 600 cm², eight small ones $8 \cdot 150 = 1200$ cm²: twice as much.

A pack is to hold 1 litre and have a square base. Try $a = 5$ cm, 8 cm, 10 cm and 12.5 cm (the height follows from the volume). For which base edge is the surface area smallest?

$a = 5$: $h = 40$, $O = 50 + 800 = 850$ · $a = 8$: $h = 15.625$, $O = 128 + 500 = 628$ · $a = 10$: $O = 600$ · $a = 12.5$: $h = 6.4$, $O = 312.5 + 320 = 632.5$. Smallest for the cube.

TEST YOURSELF!

House: cuboid 480 m³ and roof 120 m³. Enclosed volume?

$480 + 120 = 600$

A cube with a 4 cm edge with a cuboid of 4 × 2 × 3 (cm) on top: $V$ in cm³?

$64 + 24 = 88$

Eight cubes with a 5 cm edge: total surface area in cm²?

$8 \cdot 150 = 1200$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A wooden beam (pine, $\varrho \approx 0.5\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$) is 3 m long and has a square cross-section of 10 cm × 10 cm. How heavy is it?

$V = 100 \cdot 300 = 30{,}000$ cm³, $m = 15{,}000$ g = 15 kg.

A ditch (trapezium prism) is 3 m wide at the top and 1 m at the bottom, 1.5 m deep and 40 m long. The soil has a density of about 1.6 t/m³. How many tonnes of soil are dug out?

$G = \tfrac{3 + 1}{2} \cdot 1.5 = 3$ m², $V = 120$ m³, $m \approx 192$ t.

A prism has a regular hexagon as its base. It can be split into 6 equilateral triangles of about 10.4 cm² each. The prism is 8 cm high. Calculate the volume and the mass if it is made of glass ($\varrho \approx 2.5\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$).

$G \approx 62.4$ cm², $V \approx 499$ cm³, $m \approx 1248$ g ≈ 1.25 kg.

EXCURSIONNATURE

Why bees build in hexagons

A honeycomb consists of many small hexagonal prisms. As early as around AD 320, the Greek mathematician Pappus of Alexandria wondered about this and suggested that bees had a kind of “geometric foresight”: with hexagons the cells hold the most honey for the least wax.

Only three regular polygons fill the plane without gaps: triangles, squares and hexagons (more on this in the elective area). Of these three, the hexagon has the smallest perimeter for the same area – so the cell walls are shortest.

That no other division of the plane into equal areas manages with less wall length was only proved by the American mathematician Thomas Hales in 1999.

Sources: Pappus of Alexandria, “Synagoge” (Collection), Book 5; Thomas C. Hales, “The Honeycomb Conjecture”, Discrete & Computational Geometry 25 (2001).
